1	Video Analysis of Anterior Cruciate
2	Ligament Tears in Professional
3	American Football Athletes
4	Jeffrey T. Johnston,* MD, Bert R. Mandelbaum,y MD, David Schub,z MD, Scott A. Rodeo,§ MD,
5	Matthew J. Matava,|| MD, Holly J. Silvers,{ PhD, Brian J. Cole,# MD, MBA,
6	Neil S. ElAttrache,y MD, Tim R. McAdams,** MD, and Robert H. Brophy,||yy MD
7	Investigation performed at the Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis, Missouri,
8	USA, and the Kerlan Jobe Institute at Cedars Sinai, Los Angeles, California, USA
9	
10	Background: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are prevalent in contact sports that feature cutting and pivoting, such as
11	American football. These injuries typically require surgical treatment, can result in significant missed time from competition, and
12	may have deleterious long-term effects on an athlete’s playing career and health. While the majority of ACL tears in other sports
13	have been shown to occur from a noncontact mechanism, it stands to reason that a significant number of ACL tears in American
14	football would occur after contact, given the nature of the sport.
15	Hypothesis/Purpose: The purpose was to describe the mechanism, playing situation, and lower extremity limb position associ-
16	ated with ACL injuries in professional American football players through video analysis to test the hypothesis that a majority of
17	injuries occur via a contact mechanism.
18	Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
19	Methods: A retrospective cohort of National Football League (NFL) players with ACL injuries from 3 consecutive seasons (2013-
20	2016) was populated by searching publicly available online databases and other traditional media sources. Of 156 ACL injuries
21	identified, 77 occurred during the regular season and playoffs, with video analysis available for 69 injuries. The video of each injury
22	was independently viewed by 2 reviewers to determine the nature of the injury (ie, whether it occurred via a noncontact mech-
23	anism), the position of the lower extremity, and the football activity at the time of injury. Playing surface, player position, and
24	time that the injury occurred were also recorded.
25	Results: Contrary to our hypothesis, the majority of ACL injuries occurred via a noncontact mechanism (50 of 69, 72.5%), with the
26	exception of injury to offensive linemen, who had a noncontact mechanism in only 20% of injuries. For noncontact injuries, the
27	most common football activity at the time of injury was pivoting/cutting, and the most common position of the injured extremity
28	included hip abduction/flexion, early knee flexion/abduction, and foot abduction/external rotation. There was no association
29	between injury mechanism and time of injury or playing surface in this cohort.
30	Conclusion: In this study of players in the NFL, the majority of ACL tears involved a noncontact mechanism, with the lower
31	extremity exhibiting a dynamic valgus moment at the knee. These findings suggest that ACL injury prevention programs may
32	reduce the risk of noncontact ACL tears in American football players.
33	Keywords: football; anterior cruciate ligament; ACL tear; injury mechanism

Video Analysis of Anterior Cruciate
Ligament Tears in Professional
American Football Athletes
Jeffrey T. Johnston,* MD, Bert R. Mandelbaum,y MD, David Schub,z MD, Scott A. Rodeo,§ MD,
Matthew J. Matava,|| MD, Holly J. Silvers,{ PhD, Brian J. Cole,# MD, MBA,
Neil S. ElAttrache,y MD, Tim R. McAdams,** MD, and Robert H. Brophy,||yy MD
Investigation performed at the Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis, Missouri,
USA, and the Kerlan Jobe Institute at Cedars Sinai, Los Angeles, California, USA

Background: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are prevalent in contact sports that feature cutting and pivoting, such as
American football. These injuries typically require surgical treatment, can result in significant missed time from competition, and
may have deleterious long-term effects on an athlete’s playing career and health. While the majority of ACL tears in other sports
have been shown to occur from a noncontact mechanism, it stands to reason that a significant number of ACL tears in American
football would occur after contact, given the nature of the sport.
Hypothesis/Purpose: The purpose was to describe the mechanism, playing situation, and lower extremity limb position associ-
ated with ACL injuries in professional American football players through video analysis to test the hypothesis that a majority of
injuries occur via a contact mechanism.
Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: A retrospective cohort of National Football League (NFL) players with ACL injuries from 3 consecutive seasons (2013-
2016) was populated by searching publicly available online databases and other traditional media sources. Of 156 ACL injuries
identified, 77 occurred during the regular season and playoffs, with video analysis available for 69 injuries. The video of each injury
was independently viewed by 2 reviewers to determine the nature of the injury (ie, whether it occurred via a noncontact mech-
anism), the position of the lower extremity, and the football activity at the time of injury. Playing surface, player position, and
time that the injury occurred were also recorded.
Results: Contrary to our hypothesis, the majority of ACL injuries occurred via a noncontact mechanism (50 of 69, 72.5%), with the
exception of injury to offensive linemen, who had a noncontact mechanism in only 20% of injuries. For noncontact injuries, the
most common football activity at the time of injury was pivoting/cutting, and the most common position of the injured extremity
included hip abduction/flexion, early knee flexion/abduction, and foot abduction/external rotation. There was no association
between injury mechanism and time of injury or playing surface in this cohort.
Conclusion: In this study of players in the NFL, the majority of ACL tears involved a noncontact mechanism, with the lower
extremity exhibiting a dynamic valgus moment at the knee. These findings suggest that ACL injury prevention programs may
reduce the risk of noncontact ACL tears in American football players.
Keywords: football; anterior cruciate ligament; ACL tear; injury mechanism

{
 "id": "Q51",
 "sourceFile": "Video Analysis of Anterior Cruciate                                Ligament Tears in Professional American    Football               Athletes.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'Video Analysis of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tears in Professional American Football Athletes' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Case Report / Case Series",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training",
  "Rehabilitation"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "American Football"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Professional / Elite",
  "Injured Athletes"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective case series of NFL players with ACL injuries in the 2013-2016 seasons, identified from public online sources. Two reviewers independently watched video for 69 of the 77 regular-season and playoff injuries to classify mechanism, limb position and football activity. Most injuries (50 of 69, 72.5%) were noncontact, except in offensive linemen, where only 3 of 12 (25%) were noncontact.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Findings come from publicly available video, so the sample depends on what was filmed and posted, and no exposure or comparison group is available. The study cannot show whether the injuries were preventable, and it does not test any prevention program.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 72.5 percent noncontact figure as the risk for their own players, but it describes only the NFL injuries that had usable video.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Johnston JT, Mandelbaum BR, Schub D, Rodeo SA, Matava MJ, Silvers HJ, et al. Video Analysis of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tears in Professional American Football Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2018.",
  "doi": "10.1177/0363546518756328",
  "abstract": "Video analysis of 69 NFL ACL injuries from the 2013-2016 seasons, with most injuries occurring without contact and a dynamic valgus knee position.",
  "tldr": "Most ACL tears in these NFL players happened without contact, usually while pivoting or cutting. This points to noncontact mechanisms as a target for injury prevention work.",
  "methods": "Retrospective case series of NFL players with ACL injuries from three seasons, found through public online databases and media. Two reviewers independently viewed the video of each injury to record mechanism, lower limb position and football activity.",
  "findings": "Of 69 injuries with video, 50 (72.5%) were noncontact. Offensive linemen had a noncontact mechanism in 3 of 12 injuries (25%). For noncontact injuries, the most common activity was pivoting or cutting (30 of 50), and the injured limb most often showed hip abduction and flexion with early knee flexion and abduction. Noncontact proportions were similar on natural grass (75%) and artificial turf (70%), but no exposure data were available to test associations.",
  "limitations": "Retrospective and based on public video, so some injuries were not captured. Video cannot measure force, there was no comparison group, and without exposure data the authors could not say whether position, timing or surface relate to injury incidence or mechanism. The abstract gives 20% noncontact for offensive linemen while Table 4 and the results text give 25% (3 of 12); this record uses the table value.",
  "practicalImplications": "In this NFL sample, most ACL tears were noncontact, so prevention planning for cutting and pivoting athletes should include noncontact mechanisms. Offensive linemen were the exception, so their contact-related risk may need separate attention.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Cutting and pivoting were the most common activities in noncontact ACL tears, so technique work on knee and hip alignment during cuts is a reasonable focus for position-specific prevention. The paper does not test any training intervention.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study does not address rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions and should not be used to judge readiness after ACL reconstruction."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary and paper.findings: offensive linemen noncontact 20% (abstract figure) -> 3 of 12 (25%) per Table 4 and results ('a very low rate of noncontact injuries among offensive linemen (25%)')",
   "paper.findings: 'Mechanism was not associated with time of injury or playing surface' -> descriptive surface proportions only, since the authors state 'we were unable to conclude whether the variables that we studied ... are associated with the incidence or mechanism of ACL injury'",
   "paper.limitations: added the abstract versus table conflict and the lack of exposure data for association claims",
   "evidenceSummary: 'in-season injuries' -> 'regular-season and playoff injuries' ('77 occurred during the regular season and playoffs')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Abstract states no association between mechanism and time or surface, but the discussion says associations could not be assessed without exposure data; the record follows the discussion.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

5	David J. Lessley,*y PhD, PE, Richard W. Kent,y PhD, James R. Funk,y PhD, PE,
6	Christopher P. Sherwood,y MS, Joseph M. Cormier,y PhD, PE, Jeff R. Crandall,y PhD,

9	Charlottesville, Virginia, USA

11	Background: Concussions in American football remain a high priority of sports injury prevention programs. Detailed video review
12	provides important information on causation, the outcomes of rule changes, and guidance on future injury prevention strategies.
13	Purpose: Documentation of concussions sustained in National Football League games played during the 2015-2016 and 2016-
14	2017 seasons, including consideration of video views unavailable to the public.
15	Study Design: Descriptive epidemiology study.
16	Methods: All reported concussions were reviewed with all available video footage. Standardized terminology and associated def-
17	initions were developed to describe and categorize the details of each concussion.
18	Results: Cornerbacks sustained the most concussions, followed by wide receivers, then linebackers and offensive linemen. Half
19	(50%) of concussions occurred during a passing play, 28% during a rushing play, and 21% on a punt or kickoff. Tackling was
20	found to be the most common activity of concussed players, with the side of the helmet the most common helmet impact loca-
21	tion. The distribution of helmet impact source—the object that contacted the concussed player’s helmet—differed from studies of
22	earlier seasons, with a higher proportion of helmet-to-body impacts (particularly shoulder) and helmet-to-ground impacts and
23	with a lower proportion of helmet-to-helmet impacts. Helmet-to-ground concussive impacts were notable for the high prevalence
24	of impacts to the back of the helmet and their frequency during passing plays.
25	Conclusion: Concussion causation scenarios in the National Football League have changed over time.
26	Clinical Relevance: The results of this study suggest the need for expanded evaluation of concussion countermeasures beyond
27	solely helmet-to-helmet test systems, including consideration of impacts with the ground and with the body of the opposing
28	player. It also suggests the possibility of position-specific countermeasures as part of an ongoing effort to improve safety.

Video Analysis of Reported Concussion
Events in the National Football
League During the 2015-2016
and 2016-2017 Seasons
David J. Lessley,*y PhD, PE, Richard W. Kent,y PhD, James R. Funk,y PhD, PE,
Christopher P. Sherwood,y MS, Joseph M. Cormier,y PhD, PE, Jeff R. Crandall,y PhD,
Kristy B. Arbogast,z PhD, and Barry S. Myers,§ MD, PhD, MBA
Investigation performed at Biomechanics Consulting and Research (BioCore), LLC,
Charlottesville, Virginia, USA

Background: Concussions in American football remain a high priority of sports injury prevention programs. Detailed video review
provides important information on causation, the outcomes of rule changes, and guidance on future injury prevention strategies.
Purpose: Documentation of concussions sustained in National Football League games played during the 2015-2016 and 2016-
2017 seasons, including consideration of video views unavailable to the public.
Study Design: Descriptive epidemiology study.
Methods: All reported concussions were reviewed with all available video footage. Standardized terminology and associated def-
initions were developed to describe and categorize the details of each concussion.
Results: Cornerbacks sustained the most concussions, followed by wide receivers, then linebackers and offensive linemen. Half
(50%) of concussions occurred during a passing play, 28% during a rushing play, and 21% on a punt or kickoff. Tackling was
found to be the most common activity of concussed players, with the side of the helmet the most common helmet impact loca-
tion. The distribution of helmet impact source—the object that contacted the concussed player’s helmet—differed from studies of
earlier seasons, with a higher proportion of helmet-to-body impacts (particularly shoulder) and helmet-to-ground impacts and
with a lower proportion of helmet-to-helmet impacts. Helmet-to-ground concussive impacts were notable for the high prevalence
of impacts to the back of the helmet and their frequency during passing plays.
Conclusion: Concussion causation scenarios in the National Football League have changed over time.
Clinical Relevance: The results of this study suggest the need for expanded evaluation of concussion countermeasures beyond
solely helmet-to-helmet test systems, including consideration of impacts with the ground and with the body of the opposing
player. It also suggests the possibility of position-specific countermeasures as part of an ongoing effort to improve safety.
Keywords: head injuries/concussion; general sports trauma; medical aspects of sports; American football; biomechanics; gen-
eral; epidemiology

{
 "id": "Q53",
 "sourceFile": "Virtual training, real effects - A narrative review on sports performance enhancement through interventions in virtual reality.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'Virtual training, real effects: a narrative review on sports performance enhancement through interventions in virtual reality' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": [
  "Training & Performance",
  "Brain Health & Psychology"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Performance",
  "Coaching",
  "Research & Analytics"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Mixed / Unspecified"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Review of pre-post virtual reality (VR) training studies in sport. Searches of Web of Science, Google Scholar and PubMed preselected 51 articles, and 12 peer-reviewed intervention studies (aggregate N=493, novice to expert athletes) were included across target, bat and ball, goal, martial arts and balance tasks. Many studies reported significant gains in target skills, often larger than gains from passive or active control training.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 12 studies were included, across different sports, skill levels and VR systems, so no pooled effect is reported. The authors note that real-world transfer and generalizability remain unresolved. The authors label the work a narrative review even though a database search is described.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read 'many studies found significant effects' as proof that VR improves competition performance, but the included studies are pre-post designs with mixed samples.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Richlan F, Weiß M, Kastner P, Braid J. Virtual training, real effects: a narrative review on sports performance enhancement through interventions in virtual reality. Front Psychol. 2023;14:1240790.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1240790",
  "abstract": "Narrative review of 12 pre-post VR intervention studies across many sports, with aggregate N=493 novice, amateur and expert athletes, showing often significant gains in target skills.",
  "tldr": "VR training has produced real skill gains in several sports, often beating passive or conventional training. Transfer to competition is still an open question.",
  "methods": "Literature search of Web of Science, Google Scholar and PubMed, last searched July 4, 2022. Of 51 preselected articles, 12 peer-reviewed pre-post intervention studies met inclusion criteria. Study design, sport, VR technology and outcomes were extracted for a narrative summary.",
  "findings": "Included studies covered archery, bowling, curling, darts, golf, baseball, table tennis, soccer, basketball, karate, cycling and balance tasks. Many reported statistically significant effects on target skills after VR training, often outperforming passive or active control conditions, although in expert golfers a VR warm-up was followed by a significant drop in performance on the first real putt. The review also discusses neurocognitive mechanisms such as visual search and imagery.",
  "limitations": "Only 12 studies were included, and they differ in sport, skill level, VR system and outcome. Real-world transfer and generalizability are discussed as unresolved.",
  "practicalImplications": "VR training may add useful practice for perceptual-cognitive, decision-making and imagery skills in some sports. The authors conclude that general recommendations for or against VR in applied practice are premature, so use should be tied to a specific skill and checked locally.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: VR can supplement training of visual search, decision-making and imagery, and one baseball study found larger gains when difficulty was adapted to the batter. Evidence of transfer to competition comes from a few small studies, such as higher next-season on-base percentage after adaptive VR batting practice.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Most included samples were healthy; one study in university soccer players with chronic low back pain reported larger pain and wellness improvements after screen-based VR training than after isokinetic or conventional training. The review does not evaluate return to sport and should not be used for return-to-play decisions."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.rtp: 'covers healthy athletes' performance training' -> notes Nambi et al. sample with chronic low back pain ('45 university football (soccer) players with chronic lower back pain')",
   "paper.practicalImplications and paper.athleteDev: 'transfer to competition is not yet shown' and 'does not show that VR gains transfer to game performance' -> transfer evidence exists but is limited ('In-competition on-base percentage was significantly higher for adaptive VR training'; '10 out of the 12 ... assessed real-world transfer'); added authors' conclusion that 'general recommendations for or against the application of interventions in VR in applied sports practice are premature'",
   "paper.athleteDev: 'pressure-related skills' removed, since pressure training is the authors' speculation and was not tested in the included studies ('we speculate that VR training of VSB with increased sport-induced anxiety could have even greater benefits')",
   "paper.findings: added cycling to the sports list and the expert golfer warm-up decrement ('a significant decrease in performance as well as in QED only for the first real-world putt after VR training')",
   "paper.citation: 'Weiss M' -> 'Weiß M' as printed"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

    and basketball have higher measures of spatial working memory. These ﬁndings provide quantitative
    evidence of domain-speciﬁc visual expertise in athletes.

Higher overall head rotation was tied to avoidance in the two-defender condition, and more varied head movement was tied to collisions.",
31	 "screeningLimitations": "The sample is small, the setting is a virtual environment, and the outcome is head movement rather than injury. The authors state that future work is needed to confirm that VR-based training reduces collision-related injuries.",

34	  "year": 2024,
35	  "citation": "Kiefer AW, Aitcheson-Huehn N, Armitano-Lago CN, MacPherson R, Willoughby D, Silva PL, et al. Visuomotor strategies for collision avoidance in athletes: Insights from virtual reality. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.",
36	  "doi": "10.1016/j.jsams.2024.07.011",
37	  "abstract": "VR study of 39 athletes avoiding virtual defenders, where two head-scanning features were linked to whether collisions occurred.",
38	  "tldr": "Athletes who scanned more and varied their head movements more were better at avoiding virtual defenders in a VR task. This links scanning to collision avoidance but does not test injury outcomes.",
39	  "methods": "Thirty-nine healthy collegiate club or varsity contact-sport athletes (14 female) completed 48 trials in VR, pursuing a virtual target while avoiding 2 to 5 virtual defenders. Head rotations were sampled at 72 Hz. Confirmatory factor analysis built a two-factor scanning model, and linear mixed models tested its link to collision outcomes.",
40	  "findings": "The overall amount of head rotation (factor 1) was higher in avoidance interactions, but only in the two-defender condition (p = .001). 43	  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Visual scanning, meaning how often and how varied head movements are while navigating past opponents, is a plausible focus for collision-avoidance practice. The study has not tested whether training it improves on-field avoidance.",
44	  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study uses healthy athletes and does not assess return to sport or rehabilitation. It cannot be used to judge readiness after a head or collision injury."

 "evidenceSummary": "Brief laboratory report with 39 healthy collegiate club or varsity contact-sport athletes (14 female) who pursued a virtual target while avoiding 2 to 5 virtual defenders in VR, with 48 trials each. Head rotation was recorded, and confirmatory factor analysis and mixed models linked two scanning features to collision outcomes. Higher overall head rotation was tied to avoidance in the two-defender condition, and more varied head movement was tied to collisions.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample is small, the setting is a virtual environment, and the outcome is head movement rather than injury. The authors state that future work is needed to confirm that VR-based training reduces collision-related injuries.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the scanning findings as proof that head-scanning training prevents collisions or concussions, but the study shows only associations within a VR task.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Kiefer AW, Aitcheson-Huehn N, Armitano-Lago CN, MacPherson R, Willoughby D, Silva PL. Visuomotor strategies for collision avoidance in athletes: Insights from virtual reality. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.1016/j.jsams.2024.07.011",
  "abstract": "VR study of 39 athletes avoiding virtual defenders, where two head-scanning features were linked to whether collisions occurred.",
  "tldr": "In a VR navigation task, a greater amount of head rotation went with avoiding virtual defenders (only with two defenders), while a more varied pattern of head movement went with collisions. This links scanning to collision avoidance but does not test injury outcomes.",
  "methods": "Thirty-nine healthy collegiate club or varsity contact-sport athletes (14 female) completed 48 trials in VR, pursuing a virtual target while avoiding 2 to 5 virtual defenders. Head rotations were sampled at 72 Hz. Confirmatory factor analysis built a two-factor scanning model, and linear mixed models tested its link to collision outcomes.",
  "findings": "The overall amount of head rotation (factor 1) was higher in avoidance interactions, but only in the two-defender condition (p = .001). The temporal variability of head movement (factor 2) was higher during interactions that led to collision, regardless of condition (p = .01). The authors report that scanning features significantly differentiated successful from unsuccessful avoidance (p < .05).",
  "limitations": "Small sample and a virtual task, with no fear of collision or real competition present. Head rotation was used as a proxy for scanning without eye tracking, collisions were few (108 versus 1237 non-collisions), and the outcome is collisions in VR, not injury. The authors note that the results need confirmation in sport.",
  "practicalImplications": "Scanning behavior is associated with avoiding collisions in a VR task, so visual scanning may be worth including in collision-awareness training. Staff should not treat this as proof that scanning training reduces injury.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Head scanning while navigating past opponents is a plausible focus for collision-avoidance practice, but more scanning helped only in the simplest condition and more varied head movement went with collisions, so 'scan more' is not a supported cue. The study has not tested whether training scanning improves on-field avoidance.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study uses healthy athletes and does not assess return to sport or rehabilitation. It cannot be used to judge readiness after a head or collision injury."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.tldr: 'Athletes who scanned more and varied their head movements more were better at avoiding virtual defenders' -> more varied head movement went with collisions, and more head rotation went with avoidance only in the two-defender condition ('participants' F2 score was significantly higher (indexing a more richly varied structure of head movements) during interactions that led to collision'; 'but only in the condition with 2 virtual opponents')",
   "paper.athleteDev: implied that more frequent and more varied head movement is the target -> states the mixed direction of the two scanning features",
   "paper.citation: removed 'et al.' since there are exactly six authors",
   "paper.limitations: added no eye tracking ('the absence of eye tracking data makes it difficult to draw definitive conclusions') and the small number of collision events (108 total)"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Concussion-adjacent framing; findings are interaction-level associations in VR only.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

 "screeningLimitations": "Only 14 trials were included, with different doses, combinations and outcomes, and no pooled analysis is reported. Because vitamin C was often combined with other supplements, the effect of vitamin C alone is hard to isolate. The article's own DOI is not printed, so the record needs external verification.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the three positive trials as support for vitamin C, but most trials were neutral or negative, and the review advises against long-term high-dose use.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Rogers DR, Lawlor DJ, Moeller JL. Vitamin C Supplementation and Athletic Performance: A Review. Curr Sports Med Rep. 2023;22(7):255-259.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "Review of 14 randomized trials of vitamin C in athletes. Three showed reduced muscle damage markers, and 11 showed neutral or negative effects, so the authors advise against long-term high-dose supplementation.",
  "tldr": "High-dose vitamin C has mixed results, with 3 of 14 trials showing less muscle damage and 11 showing neutral or negative effects. The authors advise against long-term high-dose supplementation and recommend food sources.",
  "methods": "Review based on a PubMed search of research from the previous 10 years, which yielded 97 articles. Fourteen randomized controlled trials were included and their outcomes summarized, including muscle damage, physical performance, soreness and training adaptation.",
  "findings": "Three studies reported positive outcomes, with decreased markers of muscle damage after intense exercise; all three combined vitamin C with quercetin or vitamin E, and the authors state vitamin C alone did not appear to reduce muscle damage markers with long-term use. The other 11 reported neutral or negative effects on muscle damage, physical performance, perceived soreness or training adaptations, including blunted strength, lean mass or mitochondrial adaptations with long-term vitamin C plus vitamin E. Only two studies used vitamin C alone.",
  "limitations": "Only 14 trials were reviewed, with varied doses, combinations and outcomes. The article's own DOI is not in the text, so the record should be verified externally.",
  "practicalImplications": "Staff should not expect routine high-dose vitamin C to improve performance or reduce soreness. The authors advise food as the preferred source of antioxidants, since high-dose use may blunt training adaptations.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Based on this review, long-term high-dose vitamin C is not recommended for training support, and a nutrient-rich diet is the preferred route to antioxidants.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review does not study injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide vitamin C use during recovery from injury."
 },
 "verification": {

  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Own DOI not printed; operator should verify externally before upgrading the decision.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Owens DJ, Allison R, Close GL. Vitamin D and the Athlete: Current Perspectives and New Challenges. Sports Med. 2018;48(Suppl 1):S3-S16.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-017-0841-9",
  "abstract": "Narrative review of vitamin D in athletes, covering bone, muscle and immune roles, high-dose supplement risks, and paradoxes in Black athletes with low serum levels.",
  "tldr": "Serum vitamin D has not clearly tracked bone health in athletes, and very high supplement doses may be harmful. Thresholds may need rethinking for ethnically diverse athletes, using bioavailable vitamin D.",
  "methods": "Narrative review by the authors covering vitamin D history, biology, bone, muscle and immune function, supplementation, toxicity and ethnicity. No systematic search is described.",
  "findings": "Serum 25(OH)D has consistently failed to show a clear relationship with bone health in athletes, which may partly reflect the osteogenic effect of exercise. Vitamin D may affect recovery from damaging exercise and infection risk, and the authors' group found smaller cardiac dimensions in severely deficient athletes. The authors say data from their laboratory suggest high-dose supplementation could be problematic, and Black athletes can have low serum 25(OH)D without clear physiological consequences.",
  "limitations": "Narrative review without a described search, so evidence selection is not transparent. The review includes the authors' own laboratory data, and the article is part of an expert panel supplement with a disclosed honorarium from a PepsiCo division.",
  "practicalImplications": "Staff should not assume more vitamin D is better; the authors advise against blanket supplementation, mega doses and bolus doses in favor of an individualized decision based on status. Routine screening may be unnecessary in the absence of pathology, and where testing is warranted the authors prefer bioavailable vitamin D over total serum 25(OH)D.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The authors state vitamin D is not an ergogenic aid, so supplementation above sufficiency should not be expected to improve performance. Very high doses deserve caution because 70,000 IU per week raised a catabolite that may counteract vitamin D signaling; muscle and immune benefits rest mostly on mechanistic, observational or small trial data.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review does not evaluate return-to-play decisions or injury recovery and should not be used to guide them."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary: 'a weak link between serum 25(OH)D and bone health' -> no consistent relationship ('data have consistently failed to demonstrate any relationship between serum 25[OH]D and bone health'); added cardiac structure to the coverage list",
   "synthesisCaution: 'the review only calls for re-examining the data, not for a validated clinical test' -> the review does recommend free vitamin D assays when testing is warranted, but no gold standard exists ('If testing is warranted, practitioners should use the appropriate assays to determine bioavailable (free) vitamin D'; 'No comparison of techniques and establishment of a gold standard have yet been reported')",
   "paper.athleteDev: 'possible toxicity' -> the concern is a raised catabolite at 70,000 IU/week ('the highest dose (70,000 IU/week) also raised the product of vitamin D catabolism, 24,25[OH]D'); 'largely mechanistic' -> mechanistic, observational or small trial data",
   "paper.practicalImplications: added the authors' advice against 'blanket approaches to supplementation, mega doses of vitamin D, bolus doses' and their preference for bioavailable assays",
   "paper.findings: added the authors' observation of smaller cardiac dimensions in severely deficient athletes"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Includes cardiac and supplement-dosing content; cardiac findings come from the authors' own cross-sectional study.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

  "methods": "Narrative review of vitamin D physiology, bone health and stress fractures, with a focus on adolescents and active individuals. No systematic search is described.",

  "limitations": "Narrative review without a described search, and the evidence base is heterogeneous and largely military, older-adult or observational.   "practicalImplications": "The authors recommend vitamin D3 supplementation to maintain 25(OH)D status, especially in athletes at high risk of stress fracture, but say the data do not support a specific dose or target level.   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Vitamin D status may be one modifiable factor in stress fracture risk for endurance athletes and recruits, so checking and correcting low status in high-risk athletes is consistent with the authors' advice.
